source.title_on_document: Perspective Taking Shapes Creative Performance in Human–AI Collaboration

supplement.where: PDF pp. 39–44: Appendix and Appendix 1: Task Instructions. The methods call the latter Online Appendix 1 (pp. 9–10); no separate supplement URL is supplied.
supplement.holds: Supplementary Figure 1 (p. 39) contains forward-flow trajectories and role comparisons. Supplementary Table 1 (p. 40) supplies PIT immediate-perspective-taking APIM coefficients and standard errors for novelty, usefulness, fluency, and flexibility; Supplementary Table 2 (pp. 40–41) supplies model-fit statistics. Appendix 1 (pp. 42–44) gives participant instructions and AI system, idea-selection, and posttest prompts.

paper_design_summary: In one laboratory experiment, university students were randomly assigned to work with another human or with GPT–5–mini, taking turns to propose rubber-band uses and chair improvements; both tasks were completed by the same recruited sample in randomized task order (pp. 8–10). Blinded creativity researchers rated idea novelty and usefulness, and coders measured idea fluency, category flexibility, and within-dyad category convergence; a supplementary analysis scored semantic forward flow (pp. 13–14, 39). The paper reports both human-role comparisons and whole-dyad comparisons that include AI-generated ideas in the HAI arm.

studies.label: Laboratory collaboration experiment: alternative uses and product improvement

assignment.what_was_assigned: People were assigned to human–human (HH) or human–AI (HAI) collaboration. The collaboration condition was between people, while both tasks were completed in random order. HH pairs drew lots for first speaker; the human always spoke first in HAI (pp. 8–10).
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to the HH or HAI condition, with 57 dyads in the HH condition and 55 dyads in the HAI condition.

arms.name: Human in HAI
arms.description: Human participant collaborating with GPT–5–mini, one human per HAI dyad (p. 7, section 1.3). Initially 55 people/HAI dyads; valid task data are tabulated as 49 HAI dyads for AUT and 54 for PIT (p. 8, section 2.1; p. 15, Table 1; p. 17, Table 2; p. 21, Table 4). n_analyzed uses the larger PIT count; AUT is a smaller task-specific subset.

arms.name: Human in HH
arms.description: Human participant collaborating with another human, with no AI. Initially 114 people in 57 HH dyads (p. 8, section 2.1; p. 15, Table 1). Analyzed samples are printed as 53 HH dyads for AUT and 55 HH dyads for PIT (p. 17, Table 2; p. 21, Table 4). A standalone post-exclusion HH human count is not explicitly printed, so n_analyzed is left null rather than converting dyads into a new recorded people count.

participants.exclusions: Task-specific analyzed counts: AUT 155 people; PIT 164 people. n_analyzed records the largest reported creative-task sample (PIT), not a reported union across tasks. AUT excluded 14 people: 6 in HAI (4 did not follow instructions, 2 network failure) and 4 HH dyads (2 noncompliance, 2 network failure). PIT excluded 5 people: 1 HAI participant due to network failure and 2 HH dyads (1 noncompliance, 1 network failure). Invalid data were removed only for the affected task and valid data from the other task retained (pp. 8–9, section 2.1). This is an analysis after exclusions.
participants.who: Students recruited from Central China Normal University; the same recruited sample completed both tasks (pp. 8–10).
participants.quote: After excluding participants who did not follow the instructions in each task, 155 participants had valid data for the AUT and 164 for the PIT.
participants.locator: p. 8, section 2.1; p. 9, continuation of section 2.1; p. 1, institutional location

ai_tool.how_used: Interactive turn-taking ideation partner through an API in a custom web chat interface, rather than unrestricted chatbot use. Human and AI alternated one idea per turn, with the human first; neither questions nor evaluations were permitted by the task instructions. The AI system prompt matched the human task and limited each AI idea to 40 Chinese characters. API calls were made from 2025/11/8 to 2025/12/21; printed settings: temperature = 0.70, top_p = 1.00, presence penalty = 0.00, frequency penalty = 0.20 (pp. 9–10, sections 2.2–2.3; pp. 42–43, Appendix 1).

task.description: Same-sample tasks: Alternative Uses Task (AUT), generate unusual, novel uses for a rubber band; Product Improvement Task (PIT), generate creative improvements to a chair. The single task-type field describes AUT; PIT is product idea generation. Both tasks required alternating concise ideas with the assigned human or AI partner. The later choice of the most creative idea is described, but no distinct scored idea-selection outcome is reported (pp. 9–10, 42–44).
task.duration: AUT 10 minutes; PIT 15 minutes, randomized order with a 3-minute break (p. 10, section 2.3).

outcomes.name: AUT: mean idea novelty
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two graduate students with creativity research backgrounds independently rated every idea's novelty using the Consensual Assessment Technique on a 7-point scale, blind to condition, identity, and hypotheses. Scores were averaged over raters and then over each person's ideas; AUT ICC = 0.88 (p. 13, section 2.5). Coded expert_raters because the paper explicitly describes their creativity research expertise. The participant unit refers to the human-role contrast from the linear mixed-effects role analysis (p. 14, section 2.6). The separately labeled dyad contrast aggregates the collaborating pair, including AI-authored ideas in HAI; its unit is team and its numbers must not be treated as human-only participant means. Parenthetical dispersion values in Tables 2 and 4 are copied exactly; the tables do not explicitly label them as SD or SE. APIM variants of this same outcome, including coefficients and SEs, appear in p. 19, Table 3; those associations condition on measured perspective taking and are not additional randomized treatments.

contrasts.reported: Human in HAI versus Human in HH: t(124.63) = 2.58, p = 0.029, d = 0.47. Human-only arm means, dispersion values, and confidence intervals are not printed.

outcomes.name: AUT: immediate perspective-taking index (category convergence)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Output-coded process measure: proportion of a person's ideas sharing a conceptual category with the immediately preceding idea from the interaction partner. Two coders classified ideas independently; their proportions were averaged, Cohen's kappa = 0.97 for this AUT index (pp. 13–14, section 2.5). Unit participant applies to the human-role contrast; the separately labeled dyad variant uses team-level proportions and includes AI output. This measures convergence within the interacting dyad, not similarity among different independently working human participants; in HAI the comparison partner is AI. Coded other/with_ai, with higher/lower referring to the printed process score rather than a creative-benefit sign. The paper calls perspective taking a process variable rather than a primary creativity outcome (p. 9, section 2.2). Parenthetical values in the dyad table are not explicitly labeled as SD or SE.

contrasts.reported: Human in HAI had more immediate perspective taking than Human in HH: t(145.64) = 3.21, p = 0.005, d = 0.66.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No reuse of another paper's participants is stated. AUT and PIT are two tasks in this same experiment, not independent samples or separate studies.
sample_overlap.quote: Because the AUT and PIT data were analyzed separately, when a participant's data were invalid in one task, only the data from that task were removed, whereas their valid data from the other task were retained.

company_involvement.description: No company affiliation, funding, employment, or company research involvement is reported in the saved manuscript. Academic affiliations are printed on p. 1. Use of a commercial AI API and the disclosed OpenAI-assisted translation are described as tool use, not corporate research involvement.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author affiliations and translation note; p. 9, section 2.2

eligibility.reason: Participants were randomly assigned to AI versus a human collaboration partner (p. 8, section 2.1), in laboratory rooms (p. 10, section 2.3), so this is a lab_rct with an ai_vs_active comparison. After exclusions, the paper reports 155 people for AUT and 164 for PIT, both above the threshold (pp. 8–9). Blinded ratings and coded counts score the ideas produced while the assigned partner was available (pp. 10, 13–14), and separate human-only role contrasts are reported (pp. 17, 22). The AI was a real interaction partner for assigned human participants; this is not solely an AI-versus-human output study. Category convergence and forward flow concern within-dyad interaction rather than across-person homogenization, and there is no after_ai creative-output assessment.

one_line_finding: Humans collaborating with AI produced more novel ideas than humans collaborating with another person in AUT (d = 0.47, p = 0.029; p. 17, section 3.2.2) and PIT (d = 0.42, p = 0.045; p. 22, section 3.3.2).
open_questions: The saved PDF is an undated English translation, with no printed journal or preprint version identifier; confirm correspondence with the Chinese version of record before final extraction (p. 1).

The paper gives analyzed people totals by task, but not the unique union of people with valid data across tasks; 164 is the largest task-specific analyzed count (pp. 8–9). The HH arm's post-exclusion counts are printed as dyads, so its people count has not been reconstructed.
Tables 2 and 4 do not explicitly identify the parenthetical dispersion values as SD or SE. Their dyad-level values must not be substituted for human-only means/SDs (pp. 17, 21).
The standardizer and uncertainty for the reported human-role d values are not specified; role-specific numerical means/SDs and confidence intervals are not tabulated (pp. 17, 22–23).

Supplementary Figure 1 does not specify the semantic model/distance algorithm, aggregation and inferential unit, test, or error-bar definition; exact means and numerical effect sizes are absent (p. 39).

For atlas coding, retain the category-convergence and forward-flow measures as other/with_ai process outcomes: they compare turns within an interacting dyad, including human–AI comparisons, rather than different people's independent outputs. They should not enter an across_people diversity synthesis without a scope decision (pp. 13–14, 39).
notes: Screened 2026-10-09. Read all 814 lines of the markdown, including references and appendices, and checked recorded statistics against PDF text, extracted tables, or the rendered figure. One experiment is recorded because the same participants performed both tasks; the form contains eight primary creative-performance task/construct outcomes plus four output-coded category-convergence process outcomes and two forward-flow outcomes. Each creativity or category-convergence entry keeps human and dyad aggregation variants together; unit refers to the human-role contrast, while the separately named whole-dyad contrast has unit team. The whole-dyad comparisons include AI-generated ideas and have dyad counts, not people counts. No effect sizes or standard errors were calculated, and no graph means were estimated. The paper explicitly names novelty, usefulness, fluency, and flexibility as primary creative outcomes (p. 9); no ranking among them or preregistration is stated. Baseline creative potential, personality, collaboration tendency, general perspective-taking tendency, AI experience (Table 1, pp. 15–16), and posttask partner-perspective tendency, effort, interest, difficulty, and measured satisfaction are not scored creative outputs and are excluded from outcomes (pp. 11–12, 17–18, 21–22); satisfaction is described in methods but not reported in the results tables. Figures 4 and 7–10, Tables 3 and 5, and Supplementary Table 1 analyze the same creativity outcomes conditional on measured perspective taking, not additional interventions or outcomes; the authors explicitly state these associations are not causal evidence about perspective taking (p. 34, section 4.5). Supplementary Table 2 supplies model-fit statistics, not another outcome. Pure AI-role contrasts are not treated as separate studies. Delayed perspective taking is an earlier-turn match within the task and does not imply delayed timing or after_ai. No public data/code URL or external sample reuse is stated.
